cases.subject: The Economist's three subscription options in Dan Ariely's MIT experiment
facts: The Economist offered web-only for $59, print-only for $125 and print plus web for $125.
With all three options, 84 of 100 MIT students picked print plus web, 16 picked web-only, nobody picked print-only.
Without the print-only option, 68 picked web-only and only 32 picked print plus web.
Dan Ariely described the test in his 2008 book Predictably Irrational.
cases.lesson: An option nobody picks can still change what everybody picks.

cases.subject: The 2015 Apple Watch lineup, with an 18-karat gold Edition priced far above the Sport and steel models
facts: In 2015, the Apple Watch Sport started at $349 and the stainless steel Apple Watch at $549.
The 18-karat gold Apple Watch Edition cost $10,000 to $17,000.
The gold Edition ran the same software and did the same things as the $349 Sport.
In 2016, Apple replaced the gold Edition with a white ceramic Edition from $1,249.
cases.lesson: A $17,000 watch makes a $549 watch feel sensible.

cases.subject: Costco's hot dog and soda combo frozen at $1.50, and the membership fees that pay the bills
facts: Costco has sold a hot dog and soda combo for $1.50 since 1985.
Craig Jelinek, Costco's CEO from 2012 to 2023, recalled co-founder Jim Sinegal saying: 'If you raise the effing hot dog, I will kill you.'
In 2024, Costco raised its basic membership fee in the US and Canada from $60 to $65 a year.
In fiscal 2024, Costco collected $4.83 billion in membership fees, and its net income was $7.37 billion.
cases.lesson: The $1.50 hot dog sells the $65 membership.

cases.subject: Monthly gym contracts versus pay-per-visit passes in a study of three US health clubs
names: Paying Not to Go to the Gym
facts: Economists Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier tracked 7,752 members of three US health clubs over three years.
Members on monthly contracts paid over $70 a month and went to the gym 4.3 times a month on average.
That worked out to more than $17 per visit, while a 10-visit pass cost $10 per visit.
On average, these members gave up $600 in savings during their membership.
Their 2006 paper is called 'Paying Not to Go to the Gym'.
cases.lesson: A flat fee profits from every visit you skip.

cases.subject: A women's clothing catalog test of the same dress at $34, $39 and $44
facts: A women's clothing catalog tested the same dress at three prices: $34, $39 and $44.
Raising the price from $34 to $39 increased demand by a third.
Raising it from $34 to $44 made no difference in demand.
The authors list prices ending in 9 among the cues that signal a good deal to shoppers.
Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester reported the test in Harvard Business Review in 2003.
cases.lesson: A price ending in 9 can outsell a lower price.

cases.subject: A chocolate test where a free Hershey's Kiss beat a 14-cent Lindt truffle
facts: Dan Ariely and colleagues sold Lindt truffles for 15 cents and Hershey's Kisses for 1 cent.
At those prices, 73% of buyers chose the truffle and 27% chose the Kiss.
Then both prices dropped by 1 cent, to 14 cents and free, and 69% took the free Kiss.
Only 31% still bought the truffle, though the price gap was still 14 cents.
Ariely describes the test in his 2008 book Predictably Irrational.
cases.lesson: Free makes you stop comparing.

cases.subject: The 2019 Disney+, Hulu and ESPN+ bundle priced below the three separate subscriptions
facts: Disney+ launched in the US in 2019 at $6.99 a month.
Disney also sold Disney+, Hulu with ads and ESPN+ together for $12.99 a month.
Bought separately, Disney+, Hulu with ads and ESPN+ cost $6.99, $5.99 and $4.99, or $17.97 in total.
Disney said Disney+ had passed 10 million sign-ups one day after launch.
cases.lesson: A bundle discount often sells you things you never wanted.

cases.subject: Netflix's 2011 split of its DVD-plus-streaming plan into two separately priced plans
facts: In 2011, Netflix split its $9.99 plan for DVDs by mail plus streaming into two plans of $7.99 each.
Customers who kept both paid $15.98 a month, a 60% price increase.
Netflix lost 800,000 US subscribers in the third quarter of 2011.
CEO Reed Hastings wrote: 'I messed up. I owe everyone an explanation.'
Netflix also planned to rename its DVD service Qwikster, then dropped the idea weeks later.
cases.lesson: Split a bundle and every price starts to hurt.

cases.subject: Sony selling the 2006 PlayStation 3 below its estimated build cost
facts: In 2006, Sony launched the PlayStation 3 at $499 with a 20GB drive and $599 with 60GB.
Research firm iSuppli estimated the parts and assembly cost $805.85 and $840.35.
That meant Sony lost $306.85 on each $499 console and $241.35 on each $599 one.
The estimate did not even include the controller, cables or packaging.
Sony counted on making the money back from games.
cases.lesson: The console is the razor; the games are the blades.

cases.subject: Amazon Prime's easy sign-up and its 'Iliad' cancellation flow in the FTC case
facts: Amazon Prime launched in 2005 at $79 a year for unlimited two-day shipping.
By 2022, Prime cost $139 a year in the US.
In 2023, the FTC sued Amazon, saying it pushed people into Prime and made cancelling hard.
Amazon's internal name for the cancellation process was 'Iliad', after Homer's epic of the long Trojan War.
In 2025, Amazon agreed to pay $2.5 billion: $1 billion in penalties and $1.5 billion in refunds.
Amazon did not admit any wrongdoing in the settlement.
cases.lesson: If joining takes one click, count the clicks to leave.

cases.subject: StubHub's randomized test of showing ticket fees upfront versus only at checkout
facts: StubHub showed half of its US users ticket prices with all fees included from the start.
The other half saw the fees only at checkout.
Those who saw fees only at checkout spent 21% more and were 14% more likely to buy.
Economists published the results in the journal Marketing Science in 2021.
A US FTC rule requiring all-in prices for live-event tickets took effect in 2025.
cases.lesson: The price before fees is not the price.

cases.subject: Ticketmaster's 'in demand' pricing in the 2024 Oasis reunion ticket sale
facts: In 2024, tickets for the Oasis reunion tour went on sale in the UK and Ireland.
Some standing tickets first listed at £148.50 rose to £355 under Ticketmaster's 'in demand' pricing.
Many fans only saw the higher price after waiting hours in an online queue.
The UK's Competition and Markets Authority then opened an investigation into Ticketmaster.
cases.lesson: When demand spikes, the price can change while you wait.

cases.subject: JCPenney's 2012 switch from constant sales and coupons to everyday 'Fair and Square' prices
facts: In 2012, new CEO Ron Johnson replaced JCPenney's constant sales and coupons with everyday 'Fair and Square' prices.
That year, JCPenney's sales fell 25% and the company lost $985 million.
The board fired Johnson in 2013, after 17 months as CEO.
After he left, JCPenney brought back sales and coupons.
cases.lesson: Shoppers chase the feeling of a discount, not low prices.

cases.subject: Toblerone's 2016 UK bars that got lighter by widening the gaps between the peaks
facts: In 2016, Toblerone's 400g bar in the UK shrank to 360g, and the 170g bar shrank to 150g.
Owner Mondelez made the gaps between the chocolate peaks wider instead of raising the price.
Mondelez blamed higher costs for many ingredients.
Shoppers spotted the wider gaps, and the change made headlines worldwide.
cases.lesson: Check the weight on the pack, not just the price.

cases.subject: Starbucks' off-menu 8-ounce Short below the Tall, Grande and Venti on the board
facts: Starbucks makes an 8-ounce Short, but usually leaves it off the menu board.
The board starts at the 12-ounce Tall, then the 16-ounce Grande and the 20-ounce hot Venti.
A Short latte and a Tall latte both get one espresso shot.
In 2006, economist Tim Harford argued the hidden Short lets Starbucks charge more to customers who don't ask.
cases.lesson: The cheapest option is often the one they don't show.

cases.subject: Tesla's $35,000 Model 3 headline price and how hard that version was to buy
facts: In 2016, Elon Musk unveiled the Tesla Model 3 with a starting price of $35,000.
One week later, Tesla reported 325,000 reservations, each with a $1,000 deposit.
Tesla first built the Long Range version, which started at $44,000.
The $35,000 Standard Range version finally went on sale in 2019.
Weeks later, Tesla stopped selling it online; buyers had to call or visit a store.
cases.lesson: The advertised price is often the one you can't get.

cases.subject: De Beers' 'A Diamond Is Forever' campaign and the two-months'-salary rule for engagement rings
facts: In 1947, copywriter Frances Gerety of the N.W. Ayer agency wrote 'A Diamond Is Forever' for De Beers.
In 1999, Advertising Age named it the best slogan of the 20th century.
In the 1980s, De Beers ads told men an engagement ring should cost two months' salary.
In 1982, journalist Edward Jay Epstein argued that 'forever' also kept owners from reselling their diamonds.
cases.lesson: A suggested budget is an anchor, not a rule.

cases.subject: Supreme's small weekly drops, including a $30 logo brick in 2016
facts: In 2016, Supreme sold a red clay brick stamped with its logo for $30.
Supreme releases new items in small weekly drops, usually on Thursdays.
In 2020, VF Corporation bought Supreme for $2.1 billion.
In 2024, VF sold Supreme to EssilorLuxottica for $1.5 billion.
cases.lesson: Make it rare, and people will line up for a brick.

cases.subject: A 2008 Caltech brain-scan study of the same wines shown with different prices
facts: In a 2008 Caltech study, volunteers tasted wines while lying in a brain scanner.
One wine was labeled $5 one time and $45 another time; a second was labeled $10 and $90.
Volunteers said the same wine tasted better when it carried the higher price.
Brain areas linked to pleasure were also more active at the higher price.
Hilke Plassmann and Antonio Rangel led the study, published in the journal PNAS.
cases.lesson: A higher price can make the same thing taste better.

cases.subject: A Which? price-history check of 227 UK Black Friday deals
facts: Consumer group Which? tracked Black Friday deals on 227 products from 8 big UK home and tech retailers.
It checked each product's price history before and after Black Friday 2023.
92% of the deals were the same price or cheaper at other times of the year.
Which? published the findings in 2024.
cases.lesson: A sale sign is a claim; the price history is proof.

cases.subject: Wendy's 2024 plan to test dynamic pricing on digital menu boards, and the backlash
facts: In 2024, Wendy's CEO Kirk Tanner said the chain would test 'dynamic pricing' as early as 2025.
Wendy's planned to spend $20 million on digital menu boards.
After a public backlash, Wendy's said it would not raise prices when demand is highest.
It said it might offer lower prices at slower times of day instead.
cases.lesson: A screen menu can change prices as fast as demand.

cases.subject: MoviePass selling one movie a day for $9.95 a month, 2017 to 2019
facts: In 2017, MoviePass cut its price to $9.95 a month for one movie a day.
The average US movie ticket that year cost $8.97.
MoviePass paid theaters the full ticket price each time a member went.
It passed 3 million subscribers in 2018.
MoviePass shut down in 2019.
cases.lesson: Unlimited plans only work if most members barely use them.

cases.subject: The UK regulator's 2019 crackdown on pressure selling by six hotel booking sites
facts: In 2019, the UK's Competition and Markets Authority made 6 hotel booking sites change how they sell rooms.
The sites were Booking.com, Expedia, Hotels.com, Agoda, ebookers and Trivago.
They agreed not to give a false impression of how few rooms were left or how popular a hotel was.
They also agreed to show all compulsory charges upfront and to promote only real, current discounts.
cases.lesson: 'Only 1 left' is a sales line until proven otherwise.

cases.subject: Dollar Tree's single-price model, from $1 to $1.25, plus $3 and $5 items
facts: For 35 years, Dollar Tree's standard price was $1.
In 2019, it started adding items at $3 and $5 in some stores.
In 2021, Dollar Tree raised its standard price to $1.25, a 25% increase.
cases.lesson: One simple price can stop you from comparing.

cases.subject: Gillette's first two years selling a safety razor that needs replacement blades
facts: King C. Gillette began selling his safety razor with throwaway blades in 1903.
In its first year, Gillette sold 51 razors and 168 blades.
In 1904, its second year, it sold 90,884 razors and 123,648 blades.
Every razor sold was a customer who had to keep buying new blades.
cases.lesson: Buy the handle once, pay for the blades forever.

cases.subject: Columbia House's records-for-a-penny offers and automatic album shipments
facts: Columbia House drew new members with offers like 12 records for a penny.
Members then had to buy a minimum number of albums at regular club prices.
If members didn't say no by a deadline, the next album shipped with a full-price bill.
Columbia House's revenue peaked at $1.4 billion in 1996 and fell to $17 million by 2014.
Its parent company filed for bankruptcy in 2015.
cases.lesson: A penny up front can hide the real bill.

cases.subject: Spirit Airlines' 2010 carry-on bag fee and its stripped-down 'Bare Fare'
facts: In 2010, Spirit Airlines became the first US airline to charge for carry-on bags.
The carry-on fee was up to $45 when paid at the gate.
Spirit sold a stripped-down base ticket called the 'Bare Fare', with bags and seats as extras.
Spirit filed for bankruptcy protection in 2024 and again in 2025.
cases.lesson: The cheap fare is the bait; the bag fee pays.

cases.subject: Dollar Shave Club's $1-a-month razor subscription and its $1 billion sale
facts: In 2012, Dollar Shave Club launched, mailing razor blades to subscribers from $1 a month.
Its launch video, starring co-founder Michael Dubin, cost $4,500 to make.
The video brought in 12,000 orders in the first 48 hours.
In 2016, Unilever bought Dollar Shave Club for $1 billion.
cases.lesson: A $1 monthly price turns one sale into a habit.

cases.subject: 99 Cents Only Stores' 2008 move from 99-cent to 99.99-cent prices
facts: 99 Cents Only Stores opened in 1982, selling everything for 99 cents.
In 2008, the chain raised its prices for the first time, to 99.99 cents.
The increase was 0.99 cents, so every price still started with 99.
In 2024, the chain closed all 371 of its stores.
cases.lesson: Sellers will fight hard to keep the 99.

cases.subject: Volkswagen's money-losing Bugatti Veyron flagship, built from 2005 to 2015
facts: Bugatti built 450 Veyrons between 2005 and 2015.
The Veyron's 16-cylinder engine made 1,001 metric horsepower.
In 2013, analysts at Bernstein Research estimated Volkswagen lost €4.6 million on every Veyron sold.
Volkswagen owned Bugatti and used the Veyron to show off its engineering.
cases.lesson: Some products exist to sell the brand, not themselves.
